Abstract
Artificial life and integrative systems neuroscience increasingly seek to explain how agency is organized through development, not merely how an already-formed controller optimizes a predefined task. This article advances an interaction-centered theory that links computational generative models, which infer hidden causes and candidate action policies, with experimental ecologies, which generate the developmental histories to be explained. The framework distinguishes reward and prior preference from concern, normativity, habit, and action policy. Concerns denote system-relative dimensions of regulatory significance grounded in an agent’s organization; habits are historically acquired dispositions; and action policies remain formally defined candidates within a computational model. The code-mediated concern hypothesis proposes that events acquire functional significance when adaptor-implemented mappings make cues informative about viability-linked concerns, thereby changing inference, precision, habit, and action selection. Teleonomic and organizational accounts locate the normative force of these concerns in present self-maintaining organization rather than conscious design or backward causation. The Layered Model of Agency differentiates operative, reflective, joint, material-mediated, sign-mediated, and symbolic agency, preventing evidence for low-level control from being generalized to collective, artifact-mediated, symbolic, or phenomenal agency. 8. Discussion
The theory locates developmental agency in the historically organized system formed through agent-environment interaction rather than in an isolated controller. Computational models articulate latent causes and candidate actions, whereas experimental ecologies determine which histories, mappings, habits, and forms of coordination can arise and be identified. Concern and normativity specify why some differences matter to the system; code-mediated mappings provide one testable route by which cues acquire functional significance; and the Layered Model constrains inference from operative control to joint, mediated, symbolic, or phenomenal agency. Developmental ecology thus constrains what can emerge, while perspective-matched evidence constrains what the observations warrant.
Computational models and experimental ecologies are distinct kinds of generative model, but their coordination is methodologically productive. An ecology that preserves relevant dependencies improves identification of computational hypotheses, whereas a computational model clarifies which interventions and measurements distinguish rival developmental explanations. The shared terminology is justified only when it yields sharper empirical designs.
The proposed mechanisms do not exclude standard associative learning, dynamical systems, enactive sense-making, or active inference, which may explain many developmental effects without organic codes. The code-mediated concern hypothesis adds explanatory value only when selective mediators and physically non-necessary mappings can be identified.

9. Conclusion
Generative models of living development comprise computational models that infer hidden causes and experimental ecologies that generate causally interpretable histories. Their integration requires an account of organizational normativity, code-mediated significance, habit formation, teleonomic directionality, and layered agency. Action policy remains a formal computational construct; habits and norm-guided action describe historically organized dispositions and practices. HRIP offers an extensible architecture for testing how structured human-rat interactions shape developmental trajectories, while its inaugural implementation provides initial evidence rather than a fixed template. Across biological and artificial systems, the framework directs inquiry toward how operative, joint, mediated, and symbolic forms of agency emerge, how interventions alter them, and what evidence warrants each attribution. Functional organization and phenomenal agency remain distinct explanatory targets.

Converging evidence from neuroscience, complexity science, and psychedelic research suggests that psychiatric symptoms may be better understood as stable patterns of organization within dynamic, multilevel systems rather than as outputs of isolated biological dysfunction. Abstract
Teaching Human Physiology in undergraduate medical education requires more than the acquisition of conceptual knowledge; it demands that students develop causal explanatory frameworks linking physiological mechanisms to their clinical manifestations. Abstract
Teaching Human Physiology in undergraduate medical education requires more than the acquisition of conceptual knowledge; it demands that students develop causal explanatory frameworks linking physiological mechanisms to their clinical manifestations. Problem-Based Learning (PBL) has been proposed as a strategy to promote this integrative form of reasoning, yet evidence in preclinical physiology, particularly among first-year medical students without prior formal clinical exposure, remains limited. This quasi-experimental pre–post study evaluated the impact of a two-session PBL intervention on physiological reasoning in 135 first-year medical students at the University of Málaga. The intervention comprised six contact hours delivered across five small-group classes (25–30 students per class) organized into teams of five students and was triggered by two real cardiovascular events involving elite athletes.
